text: This country is home to the Grand Canyon, Hollywood, and the White House.
explanation: The gold pin marks Washington, D.C., the capital of the United States.

text: The world's second-largest country by area, famous for maple syrup and vast boreal forests.
explanation: Canada's capital is Ottawa — not Toronto or Vancouver.

text: Ancient Aztec and Maya ruins meet mariachi music in this land of tacos and tequila.
explanation: Mexico City is built on the ruins of the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan.

text: The world's largest island — an autonomous Danish territory mostly covered by an ice sheet.
explanation: Nuuk is one of the world's smallest capitals, home to about 20,000 people.

text: The Maya city of Tikal rises from the jungles of this Central American country.
explanation: Tikal was one of the most powerful cities of the ancient Maya world.

text: The only Central American country where English is official, famous for the Great Blue Hole.
explanation: The Great Blue Hole is a giant marine sinkhole off the Belize coast.

text: The smallest and most densely populated country in Central America.
explanation: El Salvador is the only Central American country without a Caribbean coastline.

text: The Maya ruins of Copán lie in this country, whose capital is Tegucigalpa.
explanation: Honduras means 'depths' in Spanish, named for the deep waters off its coast.

text: The largest country in Central America, with two great lakes and a chain of volcanoes.
explanation: Lake Nicaragua once hosted freshwater sharks that swam up the San Juan River.

text: This peaceful Central American country abolished its army in 1949 and is an ecotourism haven.
explanation: Costa Rica hosts about 5% of the world's biodiversity in 0.03% of its land.

text: A famous canal cuts this country in two, linking the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.
explanation: About 14,000 ships transit the Panama Canal every year.

text: The largest Caribbean island, famous for cigars, classic cars, and salsa.
explanation: Havana's old town is a UNESCO World Heritage site founded in 1519.

text: This country shares the island of Hispaniola and became the world's first Black republic in 1804.
explanation: Haiti occupies the western third of Hispaniola; its capital is Port-au-Prince.

text: Home to Santo Domingo, the oldest European-founded city in the Americas.
explanation: Santo Domingo was founded in 1496 by Bartholomew Columbus.

text: This Caribbean island is the birthplace of reggae and Bob Marley.
explanation: Jamaica has won more Olympic sprint medals per capita than almost any nation.

text: An archipelago of 700 islands where Columbus first made landfall in 1492.
explanation: Columbus landed on San Salvador island in the Bahamas on 12 October 1492.

text: This twin-island republic just off Venezuela invented the steelpan drum and calypso.
explanation: The steelpan is the only acoustic instrument invented in the 20th century.

text: The world's top emerald producer, famous for coffee and named after Christopher Columbus.
explanation: Bogotá sits at 2,640 m, one of the highest capitals in the world.

text: Angel Falls, the world's tallest waterfall, plunges nearly a kilometre in this country.
explanation: Angel Falls drops 979 m from the Auyán-tepui plateau.

text: Named after the line of latitude that crosses it, this country also owns the Galápagos Islands.
explanation: Quito sits at 2,850 m, almost exactly on the equator.

text: The Inca citadel of Machu Picchu crowns the Andes in this country.
explanation: Machu Picchu was built in the 15th century and never found by Spanish conquistadors.

text: A landlocked Andean country with the world's highest seat of government and the Uyuni salt flat.
explanation: Salar de Uyuni is the world's largest salt flat — a giant mirror after rain.

text: Tango, gauchos, and Patagonia belong to this country stretching to South America's tip.
explanation: Buenos Aires is often called the 'Paris of South America'.

text: A 4,300 km ribbon of land squeezed between the Andes and the Pacific, home to the Atacama Desert.
explanation: Parts of the Atacama Desert have never recorded rainfall.

text: This small country between Brazil and Argentina hosted the first football World Cup in 1930.
explanation: Uruguay won that first World Cup, beating Argentina 4–2 in Montevideo.

text: A landlocked country where Guaraní is co-official and the massive Itaipu Dam hums on its border.
explanation: Itaipu, shared with Brazil, is among the world's most productive hydroelectric dams.

text: South America's largest country: the Amazon, Rio's carnival, and Christ the Redeemer.
explanation: Brasília, the purpose-built capital, was inaugurated in 1960.

text: The only English-speaking country in South America, home to Kaieteur Falls.
explanation: Kaieteur Falls is one of the world's most powerful single-drop waterfalls.

text: The smallest independent country in South America, where Dutch is the official language.
explanation: Suriname is over 90% rainforest — the most forested country on Earth.

text: Home of the Eiffel Tower, the Louvre, and 400 kinds of cheese.
explanation: The Louvre is the most visited museum in the world.

text: Oktoberfest, the autobahn, and the Brandenburg Gate are icons of this country.
explanation: The Berlin Wall divided this country's capital from 1961 to 1989.

text: Tulips, windmills, and canals — much of this country lies below sea level.
explanation: About a third of the Netherlands sits below sea level, protected by dikes.

text: Its capital hosts the EU headquarters — and claims the best waffles and chocolate.
explanation: Brussels is home to both the European Commission and NATO headquarters.

text: A tiny, wealthy grand duchy wedged between France, Germany, and Belgium.
explanation: Luxembourg is the world's only remaining grand duchy.

text: Mozart's birthplace: alpine peaks, Vienna waltzes, and coffee-house culture.
explanation: Vienna regularly tops rankings of the world's most liveable cities.

text: Famous for Alpine peaks, chocolate, precision watches, and permanent neutrality.
explanation: Bern, not Zurich or Geneva, is the Swiss capital.

text: The Emerald Isle — home of Guinness, St. Patrick, and the Cliffs of Moher.
explanation: Dublin's Trinity College guards the 1,200-year-old Book of Kells.

text: Big Ben, Stonehenge, and afternoon tea belong to this island kingdom.
explanation: Stonehenge was raised in stages between about 3000 and 2000 BC.

text: ABBA, IKEA, and the Nobel Prize come from this Scandinavian country.
explanation: Stockholm is built across 14 islands connected by 57 bridges.

text: Vikings once sailed from this land of fjords and the midnight sun.
explanation: Norway's fjord-riddled coastline stretches over 100,000 km.

text: The land of a thousand lakes and saunas, where Lapland hosts Santa's village.
explanation: Finland actually has about 188,000 lakes — and more saunas than cars.

text: LEGO bricks and the Little Mermaid statue come from this small Nordic kingdom.
explanation: LEGO comes from the Danish 'leg godt' — 'play well'.

text: A volcanic island nation of geysers and glaciers with the world's northernmost capital.
explanation: Reykjavík is heated almost entirely by geothermal energy.

text: The northernmost Baltic state, a digital pioneer where Skype was born.
explanation: Estonia was the first country to allow online voting in national elections.

text: The middle Baltic state, whose capital Riga is famed for art nouveau architecture.
explanation: Riga has one of Europe's largest collections of art nouveau buildings.

text: The southernmost Baltic state — basketball-mad and first to break from the Soviet Union.
explanation: Lithuania declared independence from the USSR in March 1990.

text: Flamenco, paella, and the still-unfinished Sagrada Família cathedral.
explanation: The Sagrada Família has been under construction since 1882.

text: Port wine and the explorer Vasco da Gama hail from mainland Europe's westernmost country.
explanation: Lisbon is one of Europe's oldest cities — older than Rome.

text: Shaped like a boot, this country gave the world the Colosseum, pizza, and opera.
explanation: The Colosseum could hold more than 50,000 spectators.

text: The Acropolis crowns the capital of this birthplace of democracy and the Olympics.
explanation: The first recorded Olympic Games were held at Olympia in 776 BC.

text: Copernicus and Chopin were born in this country famous for pierogi.
explanation: Warsaw's old town was painstakingly rebuilt after World War II.

text: The Charles Bridge spans the Vltava in this beer-loving heart of old Bohemia.
explanation: Czechs drink more beer per capita than any other nation.

text: This country split peacefully from its Czech partner in 1993; its capital sits on the Danube.
explanation: Bratislava is the only capital that borders two other countries.

text: Thermal baths, goulash, and the Rubik's Cube come from this Danube country.
explanation: Budapest has more thermal springs than any other capital city.

text: Transylvania and Bran Castle — of Dracula fame — lie within its Carpathian arc.
explanation: Bram Stoker's Dracula was inspired by the Wallachian prince Vlad the Impaler.

text: This Black Sea country produces most of the world's rose oil and gave Cyrillic to the Slavs.
explanation: The Cyrillic alphabet was developed in the First Bulgarian Empire.

text: The largest country lying entirely within Europe, long called the continent's breadbasket.
explanation: Kyiv's golden-domed St. Sophia Cathedral dates from the 11th century.

text: A landlocked country of deep forests between Poland and Russia, home to the last European bison.
explanation: Białowieża Forest, shared with Poland, shelters Europe's largest bison herds.

text: A small wine country between Romania and Ukraine with cellars that stretch for kilometres underground.
explanation: Mileștii Mici holds the world's largest wine collection, in 200 km of tunnels.

text: The largest country on Earth, spanning 11 time zones from the Baltic to the Pacific.
explanation: The gold pin marks Moscow — but a pin anywhere in Russia counts.

text: Over a thousand Adriatic islands, the walls of Dubrovnik — and the necktie was invented here.
explanation: The cravat takes its name from Croatian cavalrymen of the 17th century.

text: A tiny alpine country where Lake Bled's island church sits between the Alps and the Adriatic.
explanation: Slovenia is the only country whose name contains the word 'love'.

text: The Ottoman bridge at Mostar and the spark of World War I mark this Balkan country's history.
explanation: Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated in Sarajevo in June 1914.

text: Its capital rises where the Sava meets the Danube; Novak Djokovic calls this country home.
explanation: Belgrade is one of Europe's oldest cities, fought over in some 100 battles.

text: Its name means 'black mountain,' and the Bay of Kotor cuts into its Adriatic coast.
explanation: Venetian sailors named it for its dark, forested peaks.

text: Mother Teresa was born in this small Balkan country's capital; Lake Ohrid lies on its border.
explanation: The country added 'North' to its name in 2019, settling a dispute with Greece.

text: The 'Land of Eagles,' dotted with some 170,000 concrete bunkers from its isolationist era.
explanation: Albania's communist regime built bunkers for decades — roughly one per family.

text: The pyramids of Giza and the Sphinx stand at the edge of this country's capital.
explanation: The Great Pyramid was the world's tallest structure for nearly 4,000 years.

text: Mostly Sahara, this North African country guards the Roman ruins of Leptis Magna.
explanation: Leptis Magna was one of the grandest cities of the Roman Empire.

text: Ancient Carthage stood in this country, home to Africa's northernmost point.
explanation: Carthage battled Rome in the three Punic Wars before falling in 146 BC.

text: The largest country in Africa, nine-tenths of it Sahara.
explanation: Algeria became Africa's largest country after Sudan split in 2011.

text: Marrakech, Casablanca, and the Atlas Mountains — just 14 km from Europe at its closest.
explanation: Rabat is the capital, though Casablanca is the largest city.

text: The Blue and White Nile meet in this country, which has more pyramids than Egypt.
explanation: The royal pyramids of Meroë number around 200 — nearly double Egypt's count.

text: Africa's most populous country and the home of Nollywood cinema.
explanation: Abuja replaced Lagos as Nigeria's capital in 1991.

text: Once called the Gold Coast, it was the first sub-Saharan country to win independence, in 1957.
explanation: Ghana took its name from a medieval West African empire.

text: The world's largest cocoa producer, named after the elephant tusks once traded on its coast.
explanation: Yamoussoukro's basilica is modelled on St. Peter's — and is even taller.

text: Its capital Dakar sits on mainland Africa's westernmost point.
explanation: The famous Dakar Rally originally ran from Paris to this Atlantic capital.

text: Timbuktu's ancient manuscripts and the empire of Mansa Musa belong to this Niger River country.
explanation: Mansa Musa's 14th-century gold wealth made him perhaps the richest person ever.

text: Its name means 'land of honest men,' and its capital is Ouagadougou.
explanation: The country renamed itself from Upper Volta to Burkina Faso in 1984.

text: A mostly-Sahara country named after a great river, often confused with its southern neighbour.
explanation: Niger and Nigeria both take their names from the Niger River.

text: The Niger River rises in this bauxite-rich country whose capital is Conakry.
explanation: Guinea holds the world's largest reserves of bauxite, the ore of aluminium.

text: The birthplace of vodun (voodoo) and heart of the old kingdom of Dahomey.
explanation: Porto-Novo is the official capital, though government largely sits in Cotonou.

text: One of Africa's narrowest countries — a sliver between Ghana and Benin.
explanation: Togo is only about 115 km wide but stretches 550 km inland.

text: Its capital, Freetown, was founded as a home for freed slaves; its name means 'lion mountains'.
explanation: Portuguese sailors named it Serra Lyoa for the roar of storms over its hills.

text: Africa's oldest republic, founded by freed American slaves, with a capital named after a U.S. president.
explanation: Monrovia honours James Monroe, U.S. president when the colony was founded.

text: A vast desert country where the Sahara meets the Atlantic, crossed by iron-ore trains 2 km long.
explanation: Mauritania's iron-ore train is among the longest and heaviest in the world.

text: The smallest country on mainland Africa — a sliver along a river, surrounded by Senegal.
explanation: The Gambia hugs its namesake river and is never wider than 50 km.

text: Between Senegal and Guinea lies this small Portuguese-speaking country and its Bijagós islands.
explanation: The Bijagós archipelago counts 88 islands, home to saltwater hippos.

text: The birthplace of coffee and the 3-million-year-old fossil Lucy — never colonized.
explanation: Ethiopia follows its own calendar of 13 months, about 7 years behind ours.

text: The Maasai Mara hosts the great wildebeest migration in this land of long-distance runners.
explanation: Nairobi is the only capital with a national park on its doorstep.

text: Kilimanjaro, the Serengeti, and Zanzibar all belong to this East African country.
explanation: Dodoma is the official capital, though Dar es Salaam is the largest city.

text: Called the 'Pearl of Africa,' the Nile begins its journey here at Lake Victoria.
explanation: Half the world's remaining mountain gorillas live in Uganda's forests.

text: The 'land of a thousand hills,' known for mountain gorillas and a remarkable recovery.
explanation: Kigali is regularly ranked among the cleanest cities in Africa.

text: A small, densely populated country on Lake Tanganyika, between Rwanda, Tanzania, and the DRC.
explanation: Gitega replaced Bujumbura as Burundi's capital in 2019.

text: This Horn of Africa country has the longest coastline on the African mainland.
explanation: Somalia's coast runs over 3,300 km along the Gulf of Aden and Indian Ocean.

text: The world's newest widely recognized country, born in 2011 along the White Nile.
explanation: The Sudd, one of the world's largest wetlands, swallows the White Nile here.

text: Its art-deco capital Asmara earned UNESCO status; it split from Ethiopia in 1993.
explanation: Italian colonial architects made Asmara a showcase of modernist design.

text: A tiny country guarding the strait between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden; Lake Assal is Africa's lowest point.
explanation: Lake Assal lies 155 m below sea level and is saltier than the Dead Sea.

text: Africa's second-largest country, wrapped in the Congo rainforest and rich in cobalt.
explanation: Kinshasa and Brazzaville face each other across the Congo River.

text: Its capital Brazzaville stares directly across the river at its much larger namesake neighbour.
explanation: Brazzaville and Kinshasa are the world's closest pair of capital cities.

text: Called 'Africa in miniature' for its variety, its footballers are the Indomitable Lions.
explanation: Cameroon spans beaches, desert, mountains, and rainforest in one country.

text: Landlocked at the very heart of the continent — its name says exactly where it is.
explanation: Bangui sits on the Ubangi River, a major Congo tributary.

text: Named after a great shrinking lake, it spans Sahara in the north and Sahel in the south.
explanation: Lake Chad has shrunk by roughly 90% since the 1960s.

text: Straddling the equator on the Atlantic, nearly 90% rainforest and rich in forest elephants.
explanation: Gabon shelters more than half of Africa's forest elephants.

text: The only Spanish-speaking country in Africa — its capital sits on an island.
explanation: Malabo lies on Bioko island, far from the country's mainland region.

text: Table Mountain, Nelson Mandela, and three capital cities belong to the 'Rainbow Nation'.
explanation: Pretoria, Cape Town, and Bloemfontein each host a branch of government.

text: A Portuguese-speaking Atlantic country of oil, diamonds, and the Kalandula Falls.
explanation: Kalandula Falls on the Lucala River is among Africa's largest waterfalls.

text: A butterfly-shaped copper-belt country; Victoria Falls thunders on its southern border.
explanation: Locals call Victoria Falls 'Mosi-oa-Tunya' — the smoke that thunders.

text: Named for the medieval stone city of Great Zimbabwe; it shares Victoria Falls with its neighbour.
explanation: Great Zimbabwe's stone walls were built without any mortar.

text: Its flag famously bears an AK-47; its Indian Ocean coast runs some 2,500 km.
explanation: Mozambique's flag is the only national flag featuring a modern rifle.

text: The Okavango Delta floods the Kalahari in this diamond-rich, stable democracy.
explanation: The Okavango River never reaches the sea — it fans out into the desert.

text: Home to the world's oldest desert and the towering red dunes of Sossusvlei.
explanation: The Namib Desert is thought to be at least 55 million years old.

text: The 'Warm Heart of Africa,' dominated by a vast Rift Valley lake bearing its name.
explanation: Lake Malawi holds more fish species than any other lake on Earth.

text: The world's fourth-largest island, where lemurs and baobabs evolved in isolation.
explanation: About 90% of Madagascar's wildlife exists nowhere else on Earth.

text: The 'Kingdom in the Sky' — entirely surrounded by South Africa and entirely above 1,000 m.
explanation: Lesotho is the only country lying completely above 1,000 m elevation.

text: One of the world's last absolute monarchies, renamed from Swaziland in 2018.
explanation: King Mswati III renamed the country on its 50th independence anniversary.

text: This country spans two continents; Istanbul straddles the strait between them.
explanation: Ankara, not Istanbul, has been the capital since 1923.

text: The largest country in the world without a single river, home to Mecca and Medina.
explanation: Saudi Arabia relies on oases, aquifers, and desalination instead of rivers.

text: The heart of ancient Persia, where the ruins of Persepolis still stand.
explanation: Persepolis was the ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire.

text: Mesopotamia — the land between the Tigris and Euphrates — cradle of the first cities.
explanation: Writing, the wheel, and the first code of laws emerged in Mesopotamia.

text: Its capital claims to be the oldest continuously inhabited city in the world.
explanation: Damascus has been settled for at least 11,000 years.

text: The rose-red rock city of Petra and the deserts of Wadi Rum lie in this kingdom.
explanation: Petra was carved by the Nabataeans over 2,000 years ago.

text: Jerusalem's holy sites and the shores of the Dead Sea — the lowest point on land.
explanation: The Dead Sea's surface lies about 430 m below sea level.

text: A cedar tree stands at the centre of this small Mediterranean country's flag.
explanation: The cedars of Lebanon built Phoenician ships and Solomon's temple.

text: Seven emirates united in 1971; the Burj Khalifa now towers over their largest city.
explanation: Abu Dhabi is the capital, while Dubai hosts the world's tallest building.

text: A sultanate on the Arabian Sea, famed for frankincense since ancient times.
explanation: Oman's frankincense trade routes are a UNESCO World Heritage site.

text: At the Arabian Peninsula's southern tip, it named mocha coffee and owns otherworldly Socotra.
explanation: Socotra's dragon's blood trees grow nowhere else on Earth.

text: A small oil-rich state at the head of the Persian Gulf, between Iraq and Saudi Arabia.
explanation: Kuwait's dinar is the highest-valued currency unit in the world.

text: A thumb-shaped peninsula jutting into the Gulf; it hosted the 2022 FIFA World Cup.
explanation: Qatar was the first Middle Eastern country to host the World Cup.

text: The world's largest landlocked country — endless steppe and the Baikonur Cosmodrome.
explanation: Yuri Gagarin launched into space from Baikonur in 1961.

text: The Silk Road cities of Samarkand and Bukhara shine in this doubly landlocked country.
explanation: A doubly landlocked country is surrounded only by other landlocked countries.

text: The Karakum desert and the flaming 'Door to Hell' gas crater lie in this secretive state.
explanation: The Darvaza crater has burned continuously since around 1971.

text: Mountains cover 90% of this yurt-dotted country around the alpine lake Issyk-Kul.
explanation: Issyk-Kul never freezes despite sitting 1,600 m up in the Tian Shan.

text: The Persian-speaking country of Central Asia, crossed by the high Pamir Highway.
explanation: The Pamir Highway is the world's second-highest international road.

text: The crossroads of empires, spanned by the Hindu Kush between Iran and Pakistan.
explanation: The Khyber Pass has funnelled armies and traders for over 2,000 years.

text: The world's most populous country, where the Taj Mahal gleams beside the Yamuna.
explanation: India overtook China as the most populous country in 2023.

text: K2, Earth's second-highest peak, crowns this country on the Indus River.
explanation: K2 is considered a harder climb than Everest despite being slightly lower.

text: Built on the Ganges delta, its Sundarbans mangroves hide swimming Bengal tigers.
explanation: The Sundarbans is the largest mangrove forest in the world.

text: A teardrop-shaped island off India's tip, once called Ceylon, famous for its tea.
explanation: Ceylon tea has been the island's signature export since the 1860s.

text: Mount Everest's southern face rises in this country with the world's only non-rectangular flag.
explanation: Nepal's flag is two stacked pennants, unique among nations.

text: This Himalayan kingdom measures Gross National Happiness; the Tiger's Nest clings to its cliffs.
explanation: Bhutan is carbon-negative — its forests absorb more CO₂ than it emits.

text: The Great Wall snakes across this country's north; pandas roam its bamboo forests.
explanation: The Great Wall's many sections total over 21,000 km.

text: The Land of the Rising Sun — Mount Fuji, bullet trains, and sushi.
explanation: Tokyo is the world's largest metropolitan area, with about 37 million people.

text: K-pop, kimchi, and tech giants thrive in the southern half of this divided peninsula.
explanation: Seoul's metropolitan area holds roughly half of South Korea's population.

text: The isolated northern half of a divided peninsula, sealed behind the DMZ.
explanation: The Demilitarized Zone has become an accidental wildlife refuge.

text: Genghis Khan's homeland — the world's least densely populated country, between Russia and China.
explanation: Mongolia averages just two people per square kilometre.

text: An island 180 km off China's coast, powerhouse of semiconductors, crowned by Taipei 101.
explanation: Taiwan manufactures most of the world's advanced computer chips.

text: The world's largest archipelago — 17,000 islands including Bali and Komodo.
explanation: Komodo dragons, the world's largest lizards, live only on a few Indonesian islands.

text: Golden temples and pad thai — the only Southeast Asian country never colonized.
explanation: Bangkok's full ceremonial name is one of the longest place names in the world.

text: The limestone pillars of Ha Long Bay rise off this S-shaped country's coast.
explanation: Ha Long Bay contains around 1,600 limestone islands and islets.

text: An archipelago of 7,641 islands known for jeepneys and the Chocolate Hills.
explanation: The Chocolate Hills of Bohol number over 1,200 grassy mounds.

text: Split by the South China Sea, its Petronas Towers rise over the peninsula half.
explanation: Malaysia spans the Malay Peninsula and part of Borneo island.

text: Thousands of ancient temples dot the Bagan plain in this country once called Burma.
explanation: Over 2,000 pagodas still stand at Bagan, built from the 9th to 13th centuries.

text: Angkor Wat, the largest religious monument on Earth, rises from this country's jungle.
explanation: Angkor Wat appears on Cambodia's national flag.

text: The only landlocked country in Southeast Asia, once the 'land of a million elephants'.
explanation: The Mekong River forms much of Laos's western border.

text: A tiny, oil-rich sultanate occupying two slivers of Borneo's northern coast.
explanation: The Sultan of Brunei lives in the world's largest residential palace.

text: One of the newest countries (2002), sharing its island with Indonesia and speaking Portuguese.
explanation: Timor-Leste occupies the eastern half of the island of Timor.

text: A whole continent to itself: the Outback, the Great Barrier Reef, and the Sydney Opera House.
explanation: Canberra was purpose-built as a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne.

text: Aotearoa — land of kiwis, the All Blacks, and Middle-earth film sets.
explanation: Wellington is the world's southernmost capital of a sovereign state.

text: The eastern half of the world's second-largest island, where over 800 languages are spoken.
explanation: Papua New Guinea is the most linguistically diverse country on Earth.

text: Over 300 South Pacific islands famous for rugby sevens and kava ceremonies.
explanation: Fiji won its first-ever Olympic gold in rugby sevens in 2016.

text: This South Pacific archipelago northeast of Australia includes WWII's Guadalcanal.
explanation: The Guadalcanal campaign of 1942–43 was a turning point of the Pacific war.

text: Land-diving on Pentecost Island — the ancestor of bungee jumping — began in this archipelago.
explanation: Vanuatu was jointly ruled by Britain and France as the New Hebrides until 1980.
